Lecture 10Instantaneous Rate of Change (2.1)

7 lecture · 24 textbook · 2 past exam questions

1. Instantaneous Velocity & Rate of Change2. The Derivative from Graphs
📖 شرح المحاضرة — Instantaneous Rate of Change (2.1)

الشرح فيه جزئين، بنفس ترتيب الأسئلة تحت. الفكرة كلها: كم الشي قاعد يتغير في لحظة وحدة بالضبط؟ اقري الجزء، وبعدين حلي أسئلته.

1️⃣ السرعة اللحظية ومعدل التغير (Instantaneous Velocity & Rate of Change)

معدل التغير المتوسط (Average Rate of Change = ARC) = كم تغيرت القيمة ÷ كم تغير الزمن، على فترة (Interval).

ARC = (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a)
  • مثل لما تقولين "رحت 100 km في ساعتين" ← السرعة المتوسطة 50 km/h.
  • بس عداد السيارة (Speedometer) يعطيك السرعة الحين بالضبط ← هذي السرعة اللحظية (Instantaneous velocity).

معدل التغير اللحظي (Instantaneous Rate of Change = IRC) = نفس الـ ARC بس على فترة صغيرة جداً حول النقطة. اسمه المشتقة (Derivative) ونكتبه f′(a) ونقراه "f prime of a".

f′(a) ≈ (f(a + h) − f(a)) / h    (h صغيرة، مثل 0.01 أو 0.001)
🔑 عندك قانون (Formula)؟ عوضي a و a + 0.001 بالقانون، اطرحي، واقسمي على 0.001.
🔑 عندك جدول (Table)؟ ما تقدرين تصغرين الفترة، فخذي:
• الميل يمين (Right) = (القيمة اللي بعدها − القيمة) ÷ الفرق
• الميل يسار (Left) = (القيمة − اللي قبلها) ÷ الفرق
• وأحسن تقدير = متوسطهم: f′(a) ≈ ½(ARC⁻ + ARC⁺)
مثال (Intro): الجريب فروت (Grapefruit) — كم سرعته عند t = 1 بالضبط؟

الجدول: s(0) = 6, s(1) = 90, s(2) = 142

Left (0 ≤ t ≤ 1): (90 − 6)/1 = 84 ft/sec
Right (1 ≤ t ≤ 2): (142 − 90)/1 = 52 ft/sec
52 ≤ v ≤ 84

لما نصغر الفترات حول t = 1 من الجهتين، السرعات تقرب من 68:

v(1) ≈ 68 ft/sec
مثال (Ex 1): دوا بالدم Q = 25(0.8)t، قدري معدل التغير عند t = 3

عندنا قانون، فناخذ فترة صغيرة: 3 ≤ t ≤ 3.01

ARC = (25(0.8)3.01 − 25(0.8)3) / 0.01
≈ −2.85 mg/min

التفسير (Interpretation): بعد 3 دقايق، كمية الدوا بالدم تنقص تقريباً 2.85 mg كل دقيقة. (الإشارة السالبة = تنقص)

مثال (Ex 2): قدري f′(2) إذا f(x) = x³
Interval: 2 ≤ x ≤ 2.001
((2.001)³ − 2³) / 0.001 = (8.012006 − 8) / 0.001
≈ 12.006
f′(2) ≈ 12
مثال (Ex 6): أراضي المزارع (Farm land) بالجدول
Year19801985199019952000
million acres10391012987963945

(a) المعدل المتوسط بين 1980 و 2000:

ARC = (945 − 1039) / (2000 − 1980) = −94 / 20
= −4.7 million acres/year

(b) قدري f′(1995) (متوسط اليمين واليسار):

Right: (945 − 963)/5 = −3.6
Left: (963 − 987)/5 = −4.8
f′(1995) ≈ (−3.6 + (−4.8))/2
≈ −4.2 million acres/year

يعني سنة 1995 أراضي المزارع كانت تنقص تقريباً 4.2 مليون acre بالسنة.

📏 الوحدات (Units): وحدة المشتقة دايماً = وحدة y ÷ وحدة x.
mg و minutes ← mg/min  |  parasites/µL و days ← parasites per µL per day
🗣️ جملة التفسير الجاهزة: "At t = …، الـ … is increasing (لو موجب) / decreasing (لو سالب) by about … units per …"
مثال (Past Exam 2021 Q3): طفيليات الملاريا (Malarial parasites)، قدري N′(3)

الجدول: N(2) = 2,357, N(3) = 12,750, N(4) = 26,661

ARC⁺ = (26,661 − 12,750)/1 = 13,911
ARC⁻ = (12,750 − 2,357)/1 = 10,393
N′(3) ≈ (13,911 + 10,393)/2 = 12,152

التفسير: باليوم الثالث، عدد الطفيليات يزيد تقريباً 12,152 parasites per microliter of blood per day.

التقعر (Concavity) — تحتاجينه في سؤال الاختبار الجاي:

  • مقعر لفوق (Concave up) ◡ = الميل قاعد يزيد (مثل الكوب).
  • مقعر لتحت (Concave down) ◠ = الميل قاعد ينقص (مثل القبة).
🔑 بالجدول: طالعي أرقام الـ ARC نفسها. إذا قاعدة تكبر ← Concave up. إذا قاعدة تصغر ← Concave down.
مثال (Past Exam Midterm-B Q3): السكر بالدم (Blood glucose) بعد الأكل
Interval0–3030–6060–9090–120120–150150–180180–210
ARC1.4331.100−0.433−1.167−0.833−0.2330.267

(a) الـ ARC تنقص من 1.433 لين −1.167 (لين t = 120)، وبعدين تزيد لين 0.267:

Concave down on (0, 120) ; Concave up on (120, 210)

(b) IRC عند t = 60 = متوسط الفترة اللي قبلها واللي بعدها:

IRC(60) ≈ ½(1.100 + (−0.433)) = 0.667/2
≈ 0.33 mg/dL per minute

يعني بعد 60 دقيقة من الأكل، السكر يزيد تقريباً 0.33 mg/dL كل دقيقة.

(c) القيمة الناقصة J (عند t = 60). استخدمي ARC الفترة 30–60 مع G(30) = 135:

1.100 = (J − 135)/30
J = 30(1.1) + 135
J = 168 mg/dL

تأكدي: (155 − 168)/30 ≈ −0.433 ✓

2️⃣ المشتقة من الرسم (The Derivative from Graphs)

على الرسم، فيه نوعين خطوط:

الخطشنو هوميله يساوي
القاطع (Secant line)يوصل بين نقطتين على المنحنىARC = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)
المماس (Tangent line)يلمس المنحنى في نقطة وحدةf′(a)

تخيلي إنك تمشين على المنحنى من اليسار لليمين 🚶‍♀️:

إذا الرسم عند النقطة…المشتقة
طالع (Increasing) ↗f′ > 0 (positive)
نازل (Decreasing) ↘f′ < 0 (negative)
مسطح، فوق قمة أو تحت قاع (Horizontal tangent)f′ = 0
أشد انحدار (Steeper)المشتقة أكبر بالقيمة
مثال (Ex 3): من رسم f(x) = x²، الإشارة موجبة ولا سالبة ولا صفر؟

رسم x² شكله ◡، قاعه عند x = 0. يسار الصفر نازل، يمين الصفر طالع.

f′(1): طالع ← Positive (بالأرقام: ((1.001)² − 1)/0.001 = 2.001 ≈ 2)
f′(−1): نازل ← Negative
f′(2): طالع، وأشد من x = 1 ← Positive
f′(0): المماس أفقي ← Zero
مثال (Ex 4): قدري مشتقة y = 2x عند x = 0 بالرسم وبالأرقام

بالرسم (Graphically): ارسمي المماس عند (0, 1)، والمماس يمر تقريباً بـ (0.3, 1.2). الميل = التغير بـ y ÷ التغير بـ x:

slope ≈ (1.2 − 1)/(0.3 − 0) = 0.2/0.3 ≈ 0.67

بالأرقام (Numerically):

(20.001 − 20)/0.001 ≈ 0.693
f′(0) ≈ 0.693
مثال (Ex 5): من الرسم (Figure 2.7)، موجب ولا سالب؟

لازم تعرفين كل كتابة شنو تعني على الرسم:

i. f′(1) = ميل المماس عند x = 1. الرسم طالع هناك ← Positive
ii. (f(3) − f(1))/(3 − 1) = ميل القاطع بين x = 1 و x = 3. بما إن f(3) > f(1) القاطع طالع ← Positive
iii. f(4) − f(2) = فرق الارتفاع. الرسم ينزل من 2 لـ 4، يعني f(4) < f(2) ← Negative
🔑 تذكري:
f(4) = ارتفاع (Height)  |  f(4) − f(2) = فرق ارتفاعين  |  (f(5) − f(2))/(5 − 2) = ميل قاطع  |  f′(3) = ميل مماس
⚠️ أخطاء شائعة
  • تنسين الإشارة السالبة ← سالب يعني ينقص، مو "خطأ".
  • تقسمين على عدد الخانات بالجدول بدال فرق الزمن (مثلاً 5 سنين مو 1).
  • تنسين الوحدات (Units) بالتفسير.
  • تخلطين بين f(4) − f(2) (فرق بس) و (f(4) − f(2))/2 (ميل).
🧠 كيف تعرفين نوع السؤال؟
إذا السؤال فيه…سوي
"average rate of change between … and …"(f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)
"estimate f′(a)" أو "rate at t = …" ومعك قانون(f(a + 0.001) − f(a))/0.001
"estimate f′(a)" ومعك جدولمتوسط الميل يسار ويمين
"interpret" أو "units"increasing/decreasing by … + وحدة y per وحدة x
"positive, negative or zero" من رسمطالع = +، نازل = −، أفقي = 0
"concave up / down" من جدول ARCARC تكبر = up، ARC تصغر = down
قيمة ناقصة بالجدول ومعطينك ARCعوضي بقانون ARC وطلعي المجهول

✍️ جربي حلي الأسئلة تحت بزر Solve here، والحسابات بتطلع لك على طول.

1. Instantaneous Velocity & Rate of Change

4 lecture · 14 textbook · 2 past exam questions

Lecture Question · Intro
We throw a grapefruit straight upward into the air. Table 2.1 gives its height, y, at time t.
t (sec)0123456
y = s(t) (feet)69014216215010630
What is the velocity of the grapefruit at exactly t = 1?
A. About 90 ft/sec
B. About 68 ft/sec
C. About 52 ft/sec
D. About 84 ft/sec

B. About 68 ft/sec

Average velocity on 0 ≤ t ≤ 1: (90 − 6)/1 = 84 ft/sec; on 1 ≤ t ≤ 2: (142 − 90)/1 = 52 ft/sec, so 52 ≤ v ≤ 84. Taking smaller and smaller intervals around t = 1, the average velocities on both sides get closer to 68 ft/sec. The instantaneous velocity at t = 1 is about 68 ft/sec.

Shrink the interval around t = 1 from both sides.

Lecture Question · Ex 1
The quantity (mg) of a drug in the blood at time t (minutes) is given by Q = 25(0.8)ᵗ.
Estimate the rate of change of the quantity at t = 3 and interpret your answer.
A. ≈ 2.85 mg/min: after 3 minutes, the drug is increasing by about 2.85 mg per minute
B. ≈ −12.8 mg/min: after 3 minutes, the drug is decreasing by about 12.8 mg per minute
C. ≈ −0.2 mg/min: after 3 minutes, the drug is decreasing by about 0.2 mg per minute
D. ≈ −2.85 mg/min: after 3 minutes, the drug is decreasing by about 2.85 mg per minute

D. ≈ −2.85 mg/min: after 3 minutes, the drug is decreasing by about 2.85 mg per minute

ARC on 3 ≤ t ≤ 3.01: (25(0.8)^3.01 − 25(0.8)³)/0.01 ≈ −2.85 mg/min. After 3 minutes, the quantity of the drug is decreasing by about 2.85 mg per minute.

Use a very small interval near t = 3.

Lecture Question · Ex 2
Estimate f′(2) if f(x) = x³.
f′(2) ≈ ?
A. ≈ 8
B. ≈ 6
C. ≈ 12
D. ≈ 4

C. ≈ 12

Using 2 ≤ x ≤ 2.001: ((2.001)³ − 2³)/0.001 = (8.012006 − 8)/0.001 ≈ 12.006 ≈ 12. So f′(2) = 12.

Average rate of change over a tiny interval.

Lecture Question · Ex 6
The total acreage of farms in the US has decreased since 1980. See Table 2.2.
Year19801985199019952000
Farm land (million acres)10391012987963945
a. What was the average rate of change in farm land between 1980 and 2000?
A. −4.7 million acres/year
B. 4.7 million acres/year
C. −94 million acres/year
D. −4.2 million acres/year

A. −4.7 million acres/year

ARC = (945 − 1039)/(2000 − 1980) = −94/20 = −4.7 million acres/year.

Divide by 20 years.

b. Estimate f′(1995) (average of the left and right rates) and interpret your answer in terms of farm land.
A. ≈ −4.2 million acres/year: farm land was decreasing by about 4.2 million acres per year
B. ≈ −4.8 million acres/year: farm land was decreasing by about 4.8 million acres per year
C. ≈ 4.2 million acres/year: farm land was increasing by about 4.2 million acres per year
D. ≈ −3.6 million acres/year: farm land was decreasing by about 3.6 million acres per year

A. ≈ −4.2 million acres/year: farm land was decreasing by about 4.2 million acres per year

Right slope: (945 − 963)/5 = −3.6. Left slope: (963 − 987)/5 = −4.8. Average: (−3.6 + (−4.8))/2 = −4.2 million acres/year.

Average the slopes on the left and right of 1995.

Textbook Question · Problem 3
In a time of t seconds, a particle moves a distance of s meters from its starting point, where s = 3t².
a. Find the average velocity between t = 1 and t = 1 + h if: (i) h = 0.1, (ii) h = 0.01, (iii) h = 0.001.
A. 6.6, 6.06, 6.006 m/sec
B. 6.0, 6.0, 6.0 m/sec
C. 6.3, 6.03, 6.003 m/sec
D. 3.3, 3.03, 3.003 m/sec

C. 6.3, 6.03, 6.003 m/sec

(3(1.1)² − 3)/0.1 = 6.3; (3(1.01)² − 3)/0.01 = 6.03; (3(1.001)² − 3)/0.001 = 6.003 m/sec.

Average velocity = (s(1 + h) − s(1))/h.

b. Use your answers to part (a) to estimate the instantaneous velocity of the particle at time t = 1.
A. ≈ 3 m/sec
B. ≈ 6 m/sec
C. ≈ 6.3 m/sec
D. ≈ 0 m/sec

B. ≈ 6 m/sec

As h gets smaller, the average velocity gets closer to 6: instantaneous velocity ≈ 6 m/sec.

Look at what the values approach.

Textbook Question · Problem 4
Find the average velocity over the interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 0.8, and estimate the velocity at t = 0.2 of a car whose position, s, is given by the following table.
t (sec)00.20.40.60.81.0
s (ft)00.51.83.86.59.6
Average Average velocity over 0 ≤ t ≤ 0.8?
A. 5.2 ft/sec
B. 6.5 ft/sec
C. 9.6 ft/sec
D. 8.125 ft/sec

D. 8.125 ft/sec

(6.5 − 0)/(0.8 − 0) = 8.125 ft/sec.

Change in position ÷ 0.8.

At t = 0.2 Estimate the velocity at t = 0.2 (average of the left and right rates).
A. ≈ 2.25 ft/sec
B. ≈ 6.5 ft/sec
C. ≈ 2.5 ft/sec
D. ≈ 4.5 ft/sec

D. ≈ 4.5 ft/sec

Right: (1.8 − 0.5)/0.2 = 6.5; left: (0.5 − 0)/0.2 = 2.5. Average ≈ (6.5 + 2.5)/2 = 4.5 ft/sec.

Average the left and right slopes.

Textbook Question · Problem 5
The distance (in feet) of an object from a point is given by s(t) = t², where time t is in seconds.
a. What is the average velocity of the object between t = 3 and t = 5?
A. 8 ft/sec
B. 6 ft/sec
C. 16 ft/sec
D. 4 ft/sec

A. 8 ft/sec

(25 − 9)/(5 − 3) = 16/2 = 8 ft/sec.

Divide by 2 seconds.

b. By using smaller and smaller intervals around 3, estimate the instantaneous velocity at time t = 3.
A. ≈ 3 ft/sec
B. ≈ 6 ft/sec
C. ≈ 8 ft/sec
D. ≈ 9 ft/sec

B. ≈ 6 ft/sec

3 ≤ t ≤ 3.1: 6.1; 3 ≤ t ≤ 3.01: 6.01; 3 ≤ t ≤ 3.001: 6.001 → ≈ 6 ft/sec.

The averages approach 6.

C. 63 mm³

S(6) − S(0) = 2⁶ − 2⁰ = 64 − 1 = 63 mm³.

2⁰ = 1, not 0.

63/6 = 10.5 mm³/month.

Divide by 6 months.

A. ≈ 44.4 mm³/month

6 ≤ t ≤ 6.01: ≈ 44.52; 6 ≤ t ≤ 6.001: ≈ 44.38 → ≈ 44.4 mm³/month.

Use tiny intervals at t = 6.

B. ≈ 25 (h = 0.01), then ≈ 25 (h = 0.001): f′(2) ≈ 25

Decreasing graph → negative slope.

A. f′(1) ≈ 1.0, f′(2) ≈ 1.69: the derivative is increasing, so the graph is concave up
B. f′(1) ≈ 1.69, f′(2) ≈ 1.0: the derivative is decreasing, so the graph is concave down
C. f′(1) ≈ 0, f′(2) ≈ 1.39: the graph is concave down
D. f′(1) ≈ 1.0, f′(2) ≈ 1.69: the derivative is increasing, so the graph is concave down

A. f′(1) ≈ 1.0, f′(2) ≈ 1.69: the derivative is increasing, so the graph is concave up

f′(1) ≈ (1.001 ln 1.001 − 0)/0.001 ≈ 1.0; f′(2) ≈ (2.001 ln 2.001 − 2 ln 2)/0.001 ≈ 1.69. The rate is larger at x = 2, so the graph is concave up between 1 and 2.

Increasing slope = concave up.

f(0) = 300 (million). One year has 365 × 24 × 60 × 60 = 31,536,000 seconds, so people per year = 31,536,000/11 ≈ 2,866,909 → f′(0) ≈ 2.87 million people per year.

f is in millions and t in years.

2. The Derivative from Graphs

3 lecture · 10 textbook questions

Lecture Question · Ex 3
Use the graph of f(x) = x² to determine whether each of the following quantities is positive, negative or zero.
a. f′(1)
A. Zero
B. Negative
C. Positive

C. Positive

At x = 1 the graph is increasing → f′(1) is positive. (Numerically, ((1.001)² − 1²)/0.001 = 2.001, so f′(1) ≈ 2.)

Rising graph → positive slope.

b. f′(−1)
A. Negative
B. Positive
C. Zero

A. Negative

At x = −1 the graph is decreasing → f′(−1) is negative.

Falling graph → negative slope.

c. f′(2)
A. Zero
B. Negative
C. Positive

C. Positive

At x = 2 the graph is increasing (steeper than at x = 1) → f′(2) is positive.

Rising graph → positive slope.

d. f′(0)
A. Zero
B. Positive
C. Negative

A. Zero

At x = 0 the tangent line is horizontal → f′(0) = 0.

Bottom of the parabola → flat tangent.

Lecture Question · Ex 4
Estimate the derivative of y = 2ˣ at x = 0 graphically and numerically.
f′(0) ≈ ?
A. ≈ 2 (graphically about 2)
B. ≈ 0.693 (graphically about 0.67)
C. ≈ 1 (graphically about 1)
D. ≈ 0.5 (graphically about 0.5)

B. ≈ 0.693 (graphically about 0.67)

Graphically: the tangent line passes through (0, 1) and about (0.3, 1.2): slope ≈ 0.2/0.3 ≈ 0.67. Numerically: (2^0.001 − 2⁰)/0.001 ≈ 0.693. So f′(0) ≈ 0.693.

Use a tiny interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 0.001.

Lecture Question · Ex 5
The graph of a function y = f(x) is shown in Figure 2.7. Indicate whether each of the following quantities is positive or negative, and illustrate your answers graphically.
i. f′(1)
A. Positive
B. Negative

A. Positive

f′(1) is the slope of the tangent line at x = 1. The graph is increasing at x = 1 → positive.

Rising → positive.

ii. (f(3) − f(1))/(3 − 1)
A. Negative
B. Positive

B. Positive

This is the slope of the secant line joining x = 1 and x = 3. Since f(3) > f(1), the secant line goes up → positive.

Compare heights at 1 and 3.

iii. f(4) − f(2)
A. Positive
B. Negative

B. Negative

f(4) − f(2) is the change in height from x = 2 to x = 4. Since f(4) < f(2) (the graph goes down from 2 to 4) → negative.

Compare heights at 2 and 4.

Textbook Question · Problem 1
Use the graph in Figure 2.7 to decide if each of the following quantities is positive, negative or approximately zero. Illustrate your answers graphically.
a. The average rate of change of f(x) between x = 3 and x = 7.
A. Negative
B. Zero
C. Positive

C. Positive

The ARC is the slope of the secant line from x = 3 to x = 7. Since f(7) > f(3), the secant line goes up → positive.

Compare f(7) and f(3).

b. The instantaneous rate of change of f(x) at x = 3.
A. Positive
B. Negative
C. Zero

B. Negative

The slope of the tangent line at x = 3: the graph is decreasing at x = 3 → f′(3) is negative.

Look at the direction at x = 3.

Textbook Question · Problem 2
Figure 2.11 shows N = f(t), the number of farms in the US between 1930 and 2000 as a function of year, t.
a. Is f′(1950) positive or negative? What does this tell you about the number of farms?
A. Positive: in 1950 the number of farms was increasing
B. Negative: in 1950 the number of farms was increasing
C. Negative: in 1950 the number of farms was decreasing
D. Zero: in 1950 the number of farms was constant

C. Negative: in 1950 the number of farms was decreasing

The graph is decreasing at t = 1950 → f′(1950) is negative: the number of farms was decreasing.

Falling graph → negative.

b. Which is more negative: f′(1960) or f′(1980)? Explain.
A. f′(1960), because the graph is steeper at 1960
B. They are equal, because the graph is a straight line
C. f′(1980), because there were fewer farms in 1980
D. f′(1980), because the graph is steeper at 1980

A. f′(1960), because the graph is steeper at 1960

The graph goes down faster (is steeper) at 1960 than at 1980, so f′(1960) is more negative.

Steeper downhill = more negative.

Textbook Question · Problem 6
Figure 2.12 shows the cost, y = f(x), of manufacturing x kilograms of a chemical.
a. Is the average rate of change of the cost greater between x = 0 and x = 3, or between x = 3 and x = 5? Explain your answer graphically.
A. Between x = 3 and x = 5 (≈ 0.25 vs ≈ 0.83): its secant line is steeper
B. Between x = 3 and x = 5, because the cost is higher there
C. Between x = 0 and x = 3 (≈ 0.83 vs ≈ 0.25): its secant line is steeper
D. They are equal: both secant lines have the same slope

C. Between x = 0 and x = 3 (≈ 0.83 vs ≈ 0.25): its secant line is steeper

f(0) ≈ 1, f(3) ≈ 3.5, f(5) ≈ 4. 0–3: (3.5 − 1)/3 ≈ 0.83; 3–5: (4 − 3.5)/2 = 0.25. The secant line on 0–3 is steeper (concave down graph).

Compare the slopes of the two secant lines.

b. Is the instantaneous rate of change of the cost of producing x kilograms greater at x = 1 or at x = 4? Explain your answer graphically.
A. At x = 4: the graph is steeper there
B. At x = 1: the graph is steeper there
C. At x = 4: the cost is higher there
D. They are equal

B. At x = 1: the graph is steeper there

The tangent line is steeper at x = 1 than at x = 4, so the instantaneous rate of change is greater at x = 1.

Steeper tangent = bigger rate.

c. What are the units of these rates of change?
A. Thousand dollars per kilogram
B. Kilograms per thousand dollars
C. Kilograms per year
D. Thousand dollars

A. Thousand dollars per kilogram

Units of y over units of x: thousand dollars per kilogram.

y-units per x-unit.

Textbook Question · Problem 11
The function f is given in Figure 2.13.
(a) At which of the labeled points is f′(x) positive? Negative? Zero?
A. Positive at B, D and F; negative at A and E; zero at C and G
B. Positive at A and E; negative at C and G; zero at B, D and F
C. Positive at C and D; negative at A, E and F; zero at B and G
D. Positive at C and G; negative at A and E; zero at B, D and F

D. Positive at C and G; negative at A and E; zero at B, D and F

f′ > 0 where the graph is increasing (C, G); f′ < 0 where it is decreasing (A, E); f′ = 0 at the horizontal tangents B (minimum), D (maximum), F (minimum).

Up = positive, down = negative, flat = zero.

(b) At which labeled point is f′ largest? At which labeled point is f′ most negative?
A. Largest at C; most negative at F
B. Largest at G; most negative at A
C. Largest at C; most negative at E
D. Largest at D; most negative at F

B. Largest at G; most negative at A

f′ is largest at G (going up most steeply) and most negative at A (going down most steeply).

Steepest climb and steepest drop.

Textbook Question · Problem 13
Figure 2.14 shows the graph of f. Match the derivatives in the table with the points a, b, c, d, e.
Point a f′(a) = ?
A. −0.5
B. 2
C. 0
D. 0.5

A. −0.5

a is just before the minimum (going down slowly) → −0.5.

The derivative is the slope at each point.

Point b f′(b) = ?
A. −0.5
B. 2
C. 0
D. 0.5

D. 0.5

b is just after the minimum (going up slowly) → 0.5.

The derivative is the slope at each point.

Point c f′(c) = ?
A. 0.5
B. −0.5
C. 2
D. 0

C. 2

c is where the graph is going up steeply → 2.

The derivative is the slope at each point.

Point d f′(d) = ?
A. 0.5
B. 0
C. −0.5
D. 2

B. 0

d is at the maximum → f′ = 0.

The derivative is the slope at each point.

Point e f′(e) = ?
A. −0.5
B. 2
C. −2
D. 0.5

C. −2

e is where the graph is going down steeply → −2.

The derivative is the slope at each point.

Textbook Question · Problem 15
Graph f(x) = x² and g(x) = x² + 3 on the same axes.
(a) What can you say about the slopes of the tangent lines to the two graphs at the point x = 0? x = 1? x = 2? x = a, where a is any value?
A. The slopes of g are always 3 more than the slopes of f
B. They are equal only at x = 0
C. The slopes of g are always 3 times the slopes of f
D. They are equal at every x: the tangent lines are parallel

D. They are equal at every x: the tangent lines are parallel

g is f shifted up by 3, so at each x the tangent lines are parallel: at x = 0 both slopes are 0; at x = 1 both are 2; at x = 2 both are 4; at x = a both are 2a.

A vertical shift does not change steepness.

(b) Explain why adding a constant to any function will not change the value of the derivative at any point.
A. The graph only shifts up or down, so its slopes do not change
B. Adding a constant moves the graph left or right
C. Adding a constant makes the graph steeper
D. Adding a constant changes the derivative by the same constant

A. The graph only shifts up or down, so its slopes do not change

Adding a constant shifts the graph vertically without changing its shape, so the slope (the derivative) at any point stays the same.

Same shape → same slopes.

Textbook Question · Problem 18
The function in Figure 2.15 has f(4) = 25 and f′(4) = 1.5.
Find the coordinates of the points A, B, C.
A. A = (4, 25), B = (4.2, 25.3), C = (3.9, 24.85)
B. A = (4, 25), B = (4.2, 26.5), C = (3.9, 23.5)
C. A = (4, 25), B = (4.2, 25.15), C = (3.9, 24.7)
D. A = (4, 1.5), B = (4.2, 1.8), C = (3.9, 1.35)

A. A = (4, 25), B = (4.2, 25.3), C = (3.9, 24.85)

A is on the graph at x = 4: (4, 25). B and C are on the tangent line (slope 1.5): B: y = 25 + 1.5(0.2) = 25.3 → (4.2, 25.3); C: y = 25 + 1.5(−0.1) = 24.85 → (3.9, 24.85).

Use the tangent line y = 25 + 1.5(x − 4).

Textbook Question · Problem 19
Use Figure 2.16 to fill in the blanks in the following statements about the function g at point B.
(a) g(__) = __
A. g(1.95) = 5.02
B. g(2) = −0.4
C. g(2) = 5
D. g(5) = 2

C. g(2) = 5

B = (2, 5) is on the graph of g: g(2) = 5.

The point gives input and output.

(b) g′(__) = __
A. g′(2) = 0.4
B. g′(2) = −0.4
C. g′(1.95) = −0.02
D. g′(2) = 5

B. g′(2) = −0.4

g′(2) is the slope of the tangent line through (1.95, 5.02) and (2, 5): (5 − 5.02)/(2 − 1.95) = −0.02/0.05 = −0.4.

Slope of the tangent line at B.

Textbook Question · Problem 20
Show how to represent the following on Figure 2.17.
(a) f(4)
A. The slope of the tangent line at x = 4
B. The slope of the secant line from x = 0 to x = 4
C. The distance along the x-axis from 0 to 4
D. The height of the graph at x = 4

D. The height of the graph at x = 4

f(4) is the vertical distance from the x-axis to the graph at x = 4.

A function value = a height.

(b) f(4) − f(2)
A. The horizontal distance from x = 2 to x = 4
B. The vertical distance between the heights of the graph at x = 4 and x = 2
C. The slope of the tangent line at x = 3
D. The slope of the secant line between x = 2 and x = 4

B. The vertical distance between the heights of the graph at x = 4 and x = 2

f(4) − f(2) is the difference between the heights at x = 4 and x = 2.

A difference of heights.

(c) (f(5) − f(2))/(5 − 2)
A. The height of the graph at x = 3
B. The vertical distance between x = 2 and x = 5
C. The slope of the tangent line at x = 5
D. The slope of the secant line joining the points at x = 2 and x = 5

D. The slope of the secant line joining the points at x = 2 and x = 5

It is the slope of the secant line joining the points on the graph at x = 2 and x = 5.

Rise over run between two points.

(d) f′(3)
A. The slope of the tangent line to the graph at x = 3
B. The slope of the secant line from x = 0 to x = 3
C. The height of the graph at x = 3
D. The area under the graph up to x = 3

A. The slope of the tangent line to the graph at x = 3

f′(3) is the slope of the tangent line at x = 3.

Derivative = tangent slope.

Textbook Question · Problem 21
For each of the following pairs of numbers, use Figure 2.17 to decide which is larger. Explain your answer.
a. f(3) or f(4)?
A. f(3), because f is concave down
B. f(3), because f is increasing
C. f(4), because f is increasing
D. They are equal

C. f(4), because f is increasing

The graph is increasing, so f(4) > f(3).

Increasing → later is higher.

b. f(3) − f(2) or f(2) − f(1)?
A. They are equal, because the steps are both 1
B. f(2) − f(1), because the graph rises more between x = 1 and x = 2 (concave down)
C. f(3) − f(2), because f(3) is larger
D. f(3) − f(2), because the graph rises more between x = 2 and x = 3

B. f(2) − f(1), because the graph rises more between x = 1 and x = 2 (concave down)

The graph is concave down (rises more and more slowly), so it rises more between 1 and 2 than between 2 and 3.

Concave down → rises less each step.

c. (f(2) − f(1))/(2 − 1) or (f(3) − f(1))/(3 − 1)?
A. (f(3) − f(1))/(3 − 1), because it uses a longer interval
B. They are equal
C. (f(2) − f(1))/(2 − 1): its secant line is steeper because the graph is concave down
D. (f(3) − f(1))/(3 − 1): its secant line is steeper because the graph is concave up

C. (f(2) − f(1))/(2 − 1): its secant line is steeper because the graph is concave down

The secant line from x = 1 to x = 2 is steeper than the one from x = 1 to x = 3, because the graph is concave down.

Shorter interval near the steep part.

d. f′(1) or f′(4)?
A. f′(1), because the graph is steeper at x = 1
B. f′(4), because f(4) is larger
C. They are equal
D. f′(4), because the graph is steeper at x = 4

A. f′(1), because the graph is steeper at x = 1

The graph is steeper at x = 1 than at x = 4, so f′(1) is larger.

Steeper → bigger derivative.

Lecture 11The Derivative Function (2.2)

7 lecture · 31 textbook · 3 past exam questions

1. Graphing the Derivative from the Graph of f2. The Derivative from Tables and Formulas3. Interpreting f′ and Sketching f from f′
📖 شرح المحاضرة — The Derivative Function (2.2)

بالمحاضرة اللي قبل كنا نحسب المشتقة عند نقطة وحدة. الحين نحسبها عند كل النقاط، فتصير عندنا دالة جديدة اسمها f′(x). الشرح فيه 3 أجزاء بنفس ترتيب الأسئلة تحت.

1️⃣ رسم المشتقة من رسم f (Graphing the Derivative from the Graph of f)

دالة المشتقة (Derivative function) f′(x) = ميل المماس (Slope of the tangent line) عند كل x. يعني لكل نقطة على رسم f، نسأل: "كم ميل الرسم هني؟" والجواب هو f′(x).

🔑 كيف تقرين ميل المماس من الرسم؟
① حطي مسطرة تلمس المنحنى عند النقطة (هذا المماس).
② اختاري نقطتين على المسطرة يكون فرق x بينهم 1.
③ الميل = كم طلع (أو نزل) y ← طالع = موجب، نازل = سالب.
مثال (Ex 1): قدري f′ عند x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 وارسمي f′

عند كل نقطة نقرا ميل المماس المرسوم. مثلاً عند x = −1 المماس يطلع 2 لكل خطوة وحدة ← ميله 2. وعند x = 3 ينزل 1 ← ميله −1.

x−2−1012345
f′(x)62−1−2−2−114

(ii) نرسم النقاط (x, f′(x)) ونوصلها بمنحنى ناعم:

f′ شكله U: يبدأ عالي (6)، ينزل تحت محور x (لين −2)، وبعدين يطلع (لين 4)

يعني f′ سالب تقريباً بين x = −0.5 و x = 3.5، وموجب برا هالفترة.

مثال (Ex 2): قارني رسم f′ برسم f
رسم fرسم f′
طالع (Increasing) ↗فوق محور x (f′ > 0)
نازل (Decreasing) ↘تحت محور x (f′ < 0)
قمة (Maximum) أو قاع (Minimum)f′ = 0 ← يقطع محور x

ليش؟ عند القمة أو القاع المماس أفقي، والخط الأفقي ميله صفر.

مثال (Ex 3): أي رسم من (a)–(c) هو f′؟

الطريقة: قسمي رسم f لقطع، وكل قطعة شوفي طالعة ولا نازلة:

x < −2: f نازل ← f′ < 0
x = −2: قاع ← f′ = 0
−2 < x < 2: f طالع ← f′ > 0
x = 2: قمة ← f′ = 0
x > 2: f نازل ← f′ < 0

نبي رسم: سالب، بعدين موجب بين −2 و 2، بعدين سالب، ويقطع محور x عند −2 و 2.

Graph (c)
⚠️ لا تخلطين! ارتفاع f (قيمة f(x)) شي، وميل f (قيمة f′(x)) شي ثاني.
• f أكبر شي = أعلى نقطة بالرسم.
• f′ أكبر شي = أشد طلوع بالرسم.
• f′ أصغر شي = أشد نزول (أو أي نزول إذا الباقي كله طالع أو مسطح).
مثال (Ex 7): من Figure 2.23، عند أي x من النقاط x₁…x₆؟
a. f(x) greatest ← أعلى نقطة ← x₃
b. f′(x) greatest ← أشد طلوع ← x₅
c. f(x) least ← أوطى نقطة ← x₄
d. f′(x) least ← x₃

ليش x₃؟ لأن x₃ بعد القمة بشوي، فالرسم بدا ينزل ← f′(x₃) < 0. وباقي النقاط كلها f′ ≥ 0 (عند x₆ قمة ← f′ = 0). فـ x₃ هي الوحيدة السالبة.

مثال (Past Exam Midterm-B Q7): نقاط A إلى G على رسم f
f′ > 0 (طالع): A, D
f′ < 0 (نازل): C, F
f′ = 0 (قمم B, E وقاع G): B, E, G
f′ largest (أشد طلوع): A
f′ most negative (أشد نزول): F

(b) رسم f′: موجب قبل B، صفر عند B، سالب بين B و G، صفر عند G، موجب بين G و E، صفر عند E، وبعدين سالب وايد عند F.

2️⃣ المشتقة من الجداول والقوانين (The Derivative from Tables and Formulas)

بالجدول ما عندنا رسم، فنحسب الميل بين كل قيمتين ورا بعض:

f′(a) ≈ (f(a + Δt) − f(a)) / Δt    (Right)
أحسن تقدير: f′(a) ≈ ½ (Left slope + Right slope)
🔑 Δt (دلتا تي) = الفرق بين خانتين بالجدول (مثلاً 0.1 أو 1). آخر خانة بالجدول ما بعدها شي ← استخدمي الميل اليسار.
مثال (Ex 4): تركيز دوا بالدم c(t)، سوي جدول لـ c′(t)
t00.10.20.30.40.50.60.70.80.91.0
c(t)0.840.890.940.981.001.000.970.900.790.630.41

(a) الميل يمين (Δt = 0.1):

c′(0) ≈ (0.89 − 0.84)/0.1 = 0.5
c′(0.1) ≈ (0.94 − 0.89)/0.1 = 0.5
c′(0.2) ≈ (0.98 − 0.94)/0.1 = 0.4

(b) بنفس الطريقة:

c′(0.6) ≈ (0.90 − 0.97)/0.1 = −0.7
c′(0.9) ≈ (0.41 − 0.63)/0.1 = −2.2

(c) جدول c′ كامل:

t00.10.20.30.40.50.60.70.80.9
c′(t)0.50.50.40.20.0−0.3−0.7−1.1−1.6−2.2
c′ موجب لين t = 0.3 (التركيز يزيد)، c′(0.4) ≈ 0، وبعدين c′ سالب ويصير أكثر سلبية (التركيز ينقص وأسرع وأسرع)

(d) تقدير أحسن لـ c′(0.2) = متوسط اليسار واليمين:

Left: (0.94 − 0.89)/0.1 = 0.5 ; Right: (0.98 − 0.94)/0.1 = 0.4
c′(0.2) ≈ (0.5 + 0.4)/2 = 0.45
مثال (Past Exam Final 2023 Q4): تسرب الملوثات R(t)، قدري R′(3)

الجدول: R(2) = 8, R(3) = 10, R(4) = 13

Right: (13 − 10)/1 = 3
Left: (10 − 8)/1 = 2
R′(3) ≈ (3 + 2)/2 = 2.5 (tons/month) per month

التفسير: ببداية الشهر الثالث، معدل تسرب الملوثات قاعد يزيد تقريباً 2.5 tons/month كل شهر. (لاحظي الوحدة: R نفسه معدل بـ tons/month، فمشتقته (tons/month) per month)

تخمين قانون المشتقة (Guess a formula): احسبي المشتقة عند كم نقطة، وشوفي النمط (Pattern).

مثال (Ex 5): خمني قانون مشتقة f(x) = x²
f′(1) ≈ ((1.001)² − 1²)/0.001 ≈ 2
f′(2) ≈ ((2.001)² − 2²)/0.001 ≈ 4
f′(3) ≈ ((3.001)² − 3²)/0.001 ≈ 6

النمط: الجواب دايماً ضعف x.

f′(x) = 2x
مثال (Ex 6): R(x) = 100(1.1)x، قدري R′(0) بالميل يسار ويمين الصفر
Left (−0.001 ≤ x ≤ 0): (100(1.1)0 − 100(1.1)−0.001)/0.001 ≈ 9.53
Right (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.001): (100(1.1)0.001 − 100(1.1)0)/0.001 ≈ 9.53
R′(0) ≈ 9.53

تذكري: أي رقم أس 0 = 1، يعني (1.1)0 = 1.

3️⃣ تفسير f′ ورسم f من f′ (Interpreting f′ and Sketching f from f′)

هني العكس: معطينك رسم المشتقة f′، وتبين تعرفين شكل f.

إذا f′…يعني f…
موجب (فوق محور x)طالع (Increasing)
سالب (تحت محور x)نازل (Decreasing)
= 0 ويتغير من − لـ +قاع (Minimum)
= 0 ويتغير من + لـ −قمة (Maximum)
قاعد يزيد (رسم f′ طالع)مقعر لفوق (Concave up) ◡
قاعد ينقص (رسم f′ نازل)مقعر لتحت (Concave down) ◠
🔑 نقطة الانقلاب (Inflection point) = المكان اللي يتغير فيه التقعر. على رسم f′ هي أوطى نقطة أو أعلى نقطة في رسم f′.
مثال (Past Exam Final 2023 Q3): الرسم يبين C′(t)، معدل تغير الأدرينالين (Adrenaline)

(a) وين التركيز يزيد ووين ينقص؟ طالعي إشارة C′:

0 < t < 5: C′ < 0 ← Decreasing
5 < t < 8: C′ > 0 ← Increasing

(b) عند t = 5: C′(5) = 0 ويتغير من سالب لموجب:

Local minimum عند t = 5

(c) التقعر: طالعي رسم C′ نفسه طالع ولا نازل:

0 < t < 2: C′ ينقص ← Concave down
2 < t < 6.7: C′ يزيد ← Concave up
6.7 < t < 8: C′ ينقص ← Concave down

نقاط الانقلاب عند t ≈ 2 و t ≈ 6.7 (أوطى وأعلى نقطة برسم C′).

(d) أكبر قيم للتركيز: C ينزل لين 5 وبعدين يطلع، فأكبر القيم على الأطراف:

At the endpoints t = 0 and t = 8
⚠️ أخطاء شائعة
  • تقرين ارتفاع رسم f وتحسبينه هو f′. لا! f′ = الميل مو الارتفاع.
  • لما يعطونك رسم f′: f′ موجب يعني f طالع، مو إن f موجب.
  • خط مستقيم (Straight line) ميله ثابت ← f′ خط أفقي (Horizontal line).
  • آخر خانة بالجدول: لازم تاخذين الميل يسار لأن ما فيه شي يمين.
🧠 كيف تعرفين نوع السؤال؟
إذا السؤال فيه…سوي
"Estimate f′ at … then graph f′" من رسماقري ميل المماس عند كل نقطة، وارسمي النقاط
"Which graph is f′?"طالع = فوق محور x، نازل = تحت، قمة/قاع = يقطع محور x
"f(x) greatest / least"أعلى / أوطى نقطة
"f′(x) greatest / least"أشد طلوع / أشد نزول
جدول و "estimate f′(a)"الميل يمين، أو متوسط اليسار واليمين
"Guess a formula for f′"احسبي f′ عند 1، 2، 3 ودوري النمط
معطينك رسم f′ و "increasing / decreasing"إشارة f′
معطينك رسم f′ و "concave up / down"رسم f′ نفسه طالع (up) ولا نازل (down)

✍️ جربي حلي الأسئلة تحت بزر Solve here، والحسابات بتطلع لك على طول.

1. Graphing the Derivative from the Graph of f

4 lecture · 21 textbook · 1 past exam questions

Lecture Question · Ex 1
Estimate the derivative of the function f(x) graphed in Figure 2.18 at x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Then graph f′(x).
i. f′(−2), f′(−1), f′(0), f′(1), f′(2), f′(3), f′(4), f′(5) ≈ ?
A. 2, 6, −2, −1, −1, −2, 4, 1
B. 6, 2, 0, −2, −2, 0, 1, 4
C. −6, −2, 1, 2, 2, 1, −1, −4
D. 6, 2, −1, −2, −2, −1, 1, 4

D. 6, 2, −1, −2, −2, −1, 1, 4

f′(x) = the slope of the tangent line at each point. From the tangent lines drawn on the graph: f′(−2) ≈ 6, f′(−1) ≈ 2, f′(0) ≈ −1, f′(1) ≈ −2, f′(2) ≈ −2, f′(3) ≈ −1, f′(4) ≈ 1, f′(5) ≈ 4. (For example, the tangent line at x = −1 has slope 2 and at x = 3 has slope −1.)

Read the slope of the tangent line at each x.

ii. What does the graph of f′(x) look like?
A. A U-shaped curve: positive, then negative (between about x = −0.5 and x = 3.5), then positive again
B. An upside-down U: negative, then positive (between about x = −0.5 and x = 3.5), then negative again
C. A straight line going down from left to right
D. A U-shaped curve that stays above the x-axis everywhere

A. A U-shaped curve: positive, then negative (between about x = −0.5 and x = 3.5), then positive again

Plot the points (x, f′(x)) from part (i) and join them with a smooth curve: it starts high (6), goes below the x-axis (down to −2), then rises again (to 4).

Plot the values from part (i).

Lecture Question · Ex 2
Plot the values of the derivative function calculated in Example 1. Compare the graphs of f′ and f.
a. Where f is increasing, the graph of f′ is …
A. Increasing too
B. Above the x-axis (f′ positive)
C. Below the x-axis (f′ negative)
D. On the x-axis (f′ = 0)

B. Above the x-axis (f′ positive)

Where f is increasing, f′ is positive (the graph of f′ is above the x-axis).

Rising f → positive slope.

b. Where f is decreasing, the graph of f′ is …
A. On the x-axis (f′ = 0)
B. Decreasing too
C. Below the x-axis (f′ negative)
D. Above the x-axis (f′ positive)

C. Below the x-axis (f′ negative)

Where f is decreasing, f′ is negative (the graph of f′ is below the x-axis).

Falling f → negative slope.

c. At the points where f has a maximum or a minimum, …
A. f′ is undefined (the graph of f′ has a gap)
B. f′ has a maximum or a minimum too
C. f′ is as large as possible
D. f′ = 0 (the graph of f′ crosses the x-axis)

D. f′ = 0 (the graph of f′ crosses the x-axis)

At a maximum or minimum the tangent is horizontal, so f′ = 0: the graph of f′ crosses the x-axis.

Horizontal tangent.

Lecture Question · Ex 3
The graph of f is in Figure 2.21. Which of the graphs (a)–(c) is a graph of the derivative, f′?
Which graph is f′?
A. None of them
B. (c)
C. (b)
D. (a)

B. (c)

For x < −2, f is decreasing → f′ < 0. For −2 < x < 2, f is increasing → f′ > 0. For x > 2, f is decreasing → f′ < 0. At x = −2 and x = 2 (minimum and maximum), f′ = 0. The only graph that is negative, then positive between −2 and 2, then negative is graph (c).

Find the signs of f′ on each interval.

Lecture Question · Ex 7
In the graph of f given below (Figure 2.23), at which of the labeled x-values is:
a. f(x) greatest?
A. x₃
B. x₅
C. x₆
D. x₁

A. x₃

f(x) is greatest at x₃ (the highest point of the graph).

Highest point.

b. f′(x) greatest?
A. x₃
B. x₆
C. x₅
D. x₂

C. x₅

f′(x) is greatest at x₅ (the graph is steepest going up there).

Steepest going up.

c. f(x) least?
A. x₄
B. x₁
C. x₃
D. x₅

A. x₄

f(x) is least at x₄ (the lowest point of the graph).

Lowest point.

d. f′(x) least?
A. x₆
B. x₁
C. x₄
D. x₃

D. x₃

x₃ is just past the top, so the graph is already going down there and f′(x₃) < 0. At every other labeled point f′ ≥ 0 (at x₆, the top of the right peak, f′ = 0). So f′ is least at x₃.

Which labeled point is on a falling part?

Textbook Question · Problem 1
The graph of f(x) is given in Figure 2.22. Draw tangent lines to the graph at x = −2, x = −1, x = 0, and x = 2. Estimate f′(−2), f′(−1), f′(0), and f′(2).
f′(−2), f′(−1), f′(0), f′(2) ≈ ?
A. 2.3, 3, 2.7, 0.9
B. 1, 0, −0.5, −1
C. 1, 0, 0.5, −1
D. −1, 0, 0.5, 1

B. 1, 0, −0.5, −1

x = −2: tangent through (−2, 2.3) and (−1, 3.3): slope ≈ 1. x = −1: top of the graph, horizontal tangent: f′(−1) ≈ 0. x = 0: tangent through (0, 2.7) and (1, 2.2): slope ≈ −0.5. x = 2: tangent through (2, 0.9) and (3, −0.1): slope ≈ −1. (Answers close to these are acceptable.)

f′(a) = slope of the tangent line at x = a.

Textbook Question · Problem 2
Graph the derivative of the given function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. A horizontal line at y = 2
B. A line with slope −2 through (0, 2)
C. A horizontal line at y = −2
D. A horizontal line at y = 0

C. A horizontal line at y = −2

f is a straight line through (0, 2) and (1, 0), so its slope is the same everywhere: m = (0 − 2)/(1 − 0) = −2. So f′(x) = −2 for all x: a horizontal line at y = −2.

A line has constant slope.

Textbook Question · Problem 3
Graph the derivative of the given function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. A decreasing straight line through (1, 0): f′(x) ≈ −2x + 2
B. An increasing straight line through (1, 0): f′(x) ≈ 2x − 2
C. A horizontal line at y = 1
D. A downward parabola with its maximum at x = 1

A. A decreasing straight line through (1, 0): f′(x) ≈ −2x + 2

f is increasing for x < 1 → f′ > 0; maximum at x = 1 → f′(1) = 0; decreasing for x > 1 → f′ < 0. From the tangent lines, f′(0) ≈ 2 and f′(2) ≈ −2. f is a parabola, so f′ is a decreasing straight line through (1, 0): f′(x) ≈ −2x + 2.

The derivative of a parabola is a line.

Textbook Question · Problem 4
Graph the derivative of the given function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. An upward parabola crossing the x-axis at x ≈ −3 and x ≈ 1
B. A downward parabola crossing the x-axis at x ≈ −1.6 and x ≈ 1.6
C. An upward parabola crossing the x-axis at x ≈ −1.6 and x ≈ 1.6
D. A straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 0

C. An upward parabola crossing the x-axis at x ≈ −1.6 and x ≈ 1.6

f is increasing for x < −1.6 → f′ > 0; maximum at x ≈ −1.6 → f′ = 0; decreasing for −1.6 < x < 1.6 → f′ < 0; minimum at x ≈ 1.6 → f′ = 0; increasing for x > 1.6 → f′ > 0. f is steepest going down at about x = 0 (f′(0) ≈ −1.5) and very steep going up at both ends. So f′ looks like an upward parabola crossing the x-axis at x ≈ −1.6 and 1.6.

Signs: +, −, +.

Textbook Question · Problem 5
Graph the derivative of the given function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. Positive, 0 at x ≈ −2.5, negative (lowest ≈ −1 near x = −0.5), 0 at x ≈ 1.5, then positive
B. Negative, 0 at x ≈ −0.5, positive (largest ≈ 1 near x = 1.5), then negative
C. Always positive, largest near x = −0.5
D. Negative, 0 at x ≈ −2.5, positive (largest ≈ 1 near x = −0.5), 0 at x ≈ 1.5, then negative

D. Negative, 0 at x ≈ −2.5, positive (largest ≈ 1 near x = −0.5), 0 at x ≈ 1.5, then negative

f is decreasing for x < −2.5 → f′ < 0; minimum at x ≈ −2.5 → f′ = 0; increasing for −2.5 < x < 1.5 → f′ > 0; maximum at x ≈ 1.5 → f′ = 0; decreasing for x > 1.5 → f′ < 0. f rises most steeply at about x = −0.5, so f′ is largest there (f′ ≈ 1).

Signs: −, +, −.

Textbook Question · Problem 6
Graph the derivative of the given function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. Positive, 0 at x ≈ −2.2, negative (lowest ≈ −3 near x = −0.7), 0 at x ≈ 1, positive (≈ 3 near x = 2.5), then close to 0
B. Negative, 0 at x ≈ −2.2, positive (peak ≈ 3 near x = −0.7), 0 at x ≈ 1, negative (≈ −3 near x = 2.5), then close to 0
C. Positive everywhere, with a peak of about 3 near x = −0.7
D. Negative, 0 at x ≈ −0.7, positive (peak ≈ 3 near x = 1), then negative until x = 4

B. Negative, 0 at x ≈ −2.2, positive (peak ≈ 3 near x = −0.7), 0 at x ≈ 1, negative (≈ −3 near x = 2.5), then close to 0

f is decreasing for x < −2.2 → f′ < 0; minimum at x ≈ −2.2 → f′ = 0; increasing for −2.2 < x < 1 → f′ > 0; maximum at x ≈ 1 → f′ = 0; decreasing for x > 1 → f′ < 0, and near x = 4 the graph levels off, so f′ gets close to 0. f rises most steeply at about x = −0.7 (f′ ≈ 3) and falls most steeply at about x = 2.5 (f′ ≈ −3).

Signs: −, +, −.

Textbook Question · Problem 7
Graph the derivative of the given function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. Negative for x < 0, 0 at x ≈ 0, positive for 0 < x < 3, then negative
B. Negative for x < 3 and crossing the x-axis at x ≈ 0, 0 at x = 3, then positive
C. Positive for x < 3 (but touching 0 at x ≈ 0), 0 at x = 3, then negative
D. Negative for x < 3 (but touching 0 at x ≈ 0), 0 at x = 3, then positive

D. Negative for x < 3 (but touching 0 at x ≈ 0), 0 at x = 3, then positive

f is decreasing for x < 3, except that it levels off at x ≈ 0 (horizontal tangent) → f′(x) < 0, and f′ touches 0 at x ≈ 0 without changing sign. f has a minimum at x = 3 → f′(3) = 0. f is increasing for x > 3 → f′ > 0. f is very steep going down on the left (f′ very negative) and very steep going up on the right (f′ large).

A flat spot without a turn → f′ touches 0.

Textbook Question · Problem 10
In the graph of f in Figure 2.23, at which of the labeled x-values is
a. f(x) greatest?
A. x₅
B. x₃
C. x₁
D. x₆

B. x₃

f(x) is greatest at x₃ (the highest point of the graph).

Highest point.

b. f(x) least?
A. x₅
B. x₁
C. x₄
D. x₃

C. x₄

f(x) is least at x₄ (the lowest point of the graph).

Lowest point.

c. f′(x) greatest?
A. x₅
B. x₆
C. x₃
D. x₂

A. x₅

f′(x) is greatest at x₅ (the graph is steepest going up).

Steepest going up.

d. f′(x) least?
A. x₃
B. x₁
C. x₄
D. x₆

A. x₃

x₃ is just past the top, so the graph is already going down and f′(x₃) < 0. At every other labeled point f′ ≥ 0.

Which labeled point is on a falling part?

Textbook Question · Problem 11
Sketch the graph of the derivative of the function shown. Be sure your sketch is consistent with the important features of the graph of the original function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. A horizontal line at y = 1.5
B. A horizontal line at y = −1.5
C. A horizontal line at y = 3
D. A decreasing line through (2, 0)

B. A horizontal line at y = −1.5

f is a straight line through (0, 3) and (2, 0): m = (0 − 3)/(2 − 0) = −1.5. So f′(x) = −1.5 for all x: a horizontal line at y = −1.5.

A line has constant slope.

Textbook Question · Problem 12
Sketch the graph of the derivative of the function shown. Be sure your sketch is consistent with the important features of the graph of the original function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. A horizontal line at y = 2
B. A horizontal line at y = −1
C. A decreasing line through (1, 0)
D. A horizontal line at y = −2

D. A horizontal line at y = −2

f is a straight line through (0, 2) and (1, 0): m = (0 − 2)/(1 − 0) = −2. So f′(x) = −2 for all x: a horizontal line at y = −2.

A line has constant slope.

Textbook Question · Problem 13
Sketch the graph of the derivative of the function shown. Be sure your sketch is consistent with the important features of the graph of the original function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. An increasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 4
B. An upward parabola with its minimum at x = 2
C. An increasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 2
D. A decreasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 2

C. An increasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 2

f is decreasing for x < 2 → f′ < 0; minimum at x = 2 → f′(2) = 0; increasing for x > 2 → f′ > 0. f is a parabola, so f′ is an increasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 2.

Derivative of a parabola is a line.

Textbook Question · Problem 14
Sketch the graph of the derivative of the function shown. Be sure your sketch is consistent with the important features of the graph of the original function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. An increasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 1
B. A downward parabola with its maximum at x = 1
C. A decreasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 2
D. A decreasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 1

D. A decreasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 1

f is increasing for x < 1 → f′ > 0; maximum at x = 1 → f′(1) = 0; decreasing for x > 1 → f′ < 0. f is a parabola, so f′ is a decreasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x = 1.

Derivative of a parabola is a line.

Textbook Question · Problem 15
Sketch the graph of the derivative of the function shown. Be sure your sketch is consistent with the important features of the graph of the original function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. It crosses the x-axis three times (x ≈ −1.5, 0, 1.5) with signs −, +, −, +
B. It crosses the x-axis three times (x ≈ −1.5, 0, 1.5) with signs +, −, +, −
C. It crosses the x-axis four times (x ≈ −2, −1.5, 1.5, 2) with signs +, −, +, −, +
D. It crosses the x-axis twice (x ≈ −2, 2) with signs −, +, −

A. It crosses the x-axis three times (x ≈ −1.5, 0, 1.5) with signs −, +, −, +

f is decreasing, then has a minimum at x ≈ −1.5 → f′ < 0, then f′ = 0. f is increasing up to a maximum at x = 0 → f′ > 0, then f′(0) = 0. f is decreasing to a minimum at x ≈ 1.5 → f′ < 0, then f′ = 0. f is increasing after x ≈ 1.5 → f′ > 0. So f′ crosses the x-axis three times with signs −, +, −, +.

Each max/min of f is a zero of f′.

Textbook Question · Problem 16
Sketch the graph of the derivative of the function shown. Be sure your sketch is consistent with the important features of the graph of the original function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. A straight increasing line crossing the x-axis at x = 0
B. Upside-down U, always ≤ 0, touching the x-axis at x = 0
C. U-shaped, always ≥ 0, touching the x-axis at x = 0
D. A horizontal line above the x-axis

C. U-shaped, always ≥ 0, touching the x-axis at x = 0

f is increasing everywhere → f′(x) ≥ 0. At x = 0 the graph is flat (horizontal tangent) → f′(0) = 0. The graph gets steeper as we move away from 0 in both directions, so f′ gets larger: f′ touches the x-axis at 0 and is U-shaped.

Flat at 0, steeper on both sides.

Textbook Question · Problem 17
Sketch the graph of the derivative of the function shown. Be sure your sketch is consistent with the important features of the graph of the original function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. A decreasing straight line crossing the x-axis at the peak
B. A positive constant (horizontal line), then a negative constant; not defined at the peak
C. A negative constant, then a positive constant; not defined at the peak
D. A positive constant, then 0 at the peak, then a positive constant again

B. A positive constant (horizontal line), then a negative constant; not defined at the peak

f is made of two straight lines. On the left piece, f is increasing with a constant slope → f′ is a positive constant. On the right piece, f is decreasing with a constant slope → f′ is a negative constant. At the peak (the corner) the slope changes suddenly, so f′ is not defined there (open circles).

Each straight piece has a constant slope.

Textbook Question · Problem 18
Sketch the graph of the derivative of the function shown. Be sure your sketch is consistent with the important features of the graph of the original function.
What is the graph of f′?
A. Negative, 0 at the minimum, then positive but getting smaller near the right end
B. Negative, 0 at the minimum, then positive and getting larger near the right end
C. Always negative, closest to 0 at the minimum
D. Positive, 0 at the minimum, then negative but getting closer to 0 near the right end

A. Negative, 0 at the minimum, then positive but getting smaller near the right end

f is decreasing at first → f′ < 0. f has a minimum → f′ = 0 there. f is increasing after the minimum → f′ > 0. Near the right end, the graph of f levels off (it rises more slowly), so f′ is positive but getting smaller.

Leveling off → f′ heads toward 0.

Textbook Question · Problem 21
Match the function with one of the derivatives in Figure 2.24.
Which graph is f′?
A. (II)
B. (I)
C. (VIII)
D. (III)

C. (VIII)

f is decreasing, has a minimum at about x = −1.3, is increasing, has a maximum at about x = 1, then is decreasing. So f′ is negative, then 0, positive, 0, then negative again: f′ is positive only on a short interval in the middle. This matches graph (VIII), a narrow downward parabola that is positive only near x = 0.

Signs: −, +, −.

Textbook Question · Problem 22
Match the function with one of the derivatives in Figure 2.24. (Figure 2.24 is given in Problem 21.)
Which graph is f′?
A. (VII)
B. (V)
C. (II)
D. (IV)

D. (IV)

f is a decreasing straight line, so its slope is a negative constant (about −3). f′ is a horizontal line below the x-axis → graph (IV).

A line → constant derivative.

Textbook Question · Problem 23
Match the function with one of the derivatives in Figure 2.24. (Figure 2.24 is given in Problem 21.)
Which graph is f′?
A. (IV)
B. (II)
C. (VIII)
D. (VII)

B. (II)

f is a downward parabola crossing the x-axis at about x = 0 and x = 4: increasing for x < 2, maximum at x ≈ 2, decreasing for x > 2. So f′ is a decreasing straight line crossing the x-axis at x ≈ 2 → graph (II). (Graph (VII) crosses at a negative x, so it does not match.)

Where does the line cross the x-axis?

Textbook Question · Problem 24
Match the function with one of the derivatives in Figure 2.24. (Figure 2.24 is given in Problem 21.)
Which graph is f′?
A. (VI)
B. (V)
C. (I)
D. (III)

A. (VI)

f increases very steeply, has a maximum at about x = −2, then decreases and levels off toward y = 2. So f′ is large and positive, crosses 0 at about x = −2, is slightly negative, and then approaches 0 (not 2!) → graph (VI).

A horizontal asymptote of f → f′ goes to 0.

Textbook Question · Problem 30
Match each of the following descriptions of a function with one of the following graphs.
a. f′(1) > 0 and f′ is always decreasing
A. (II)
B. (III)
C. (IV)
D. (I)

B. (III)

f′(1) > 0 means the graph is going up at x = 1. f′ always decreasing means the graph bends downward (concave down) → graph (III).

Going up and concave down.

b. f′(1) > 0 and f′ is always increasing
A. (IV)
B. (I)
C. (III)
D. (II)

D. (II)

Going up at x = 1 and bending upward (concave up) → graph (II).

Going up and concave up.

c. f′(1) < 0 and f′ is always decreasing
A. (I)
B. (II)
C. (IV)
D. (III)

C. (IV)

Going down at x = 1 and bending downward (concave down) → graph (IV).

Going down and concave down.

d. f′(1) < 0 and f′ is always increasing
A. (IV)
B. (II)
C. (III)
D. (I)

D. (I)

Going down at x = 1 and bending upward (concave up) → graph (I).

Going down and concave up.

Past Exam Question · Midterm-B Q7
Consider the function f(x) shown in the figure below.
a. (i) At which of the labeled point(s) is the derivative f′(x) positive?
A. B, E, G
B. A, D

D. C, F

B. A, D

f′ is the slope at each point: positive at A and D (the graph is going up).

Going up.

a. (ii) At which labeled point(s) is f′(x) negative?
A. A, D
B. B, E, G
C. C, F
D. C, G, F

C. C, F

Negative at C and F (the graph is going down).

Going down.

a. (iii) At which labeled point(s) is f′(x) zero?
A. B, E, G
B. C, F
C. B, C, E
D. A, D

A. B, E, G

B and E are maximums and G is a minimum (horizontal tangent) → f′ = 0.

Peaks and valleys.

a. (iv) At which labeled point is f′(x) largest?
A. E
B. D
C. B
D. A

D. A

A is on the steepest rising part → f′ is largest at A.

Steepest going up.

a. (v) At which labeled point is f′(x) most negative?
A. F
B. E
C. C
D. G

A. F

F is on the steepest falling part → f′ is most negative at F.

Steepest going down.

b. Which describes the graph of the derivative f′(x)?
A. Positive everywhere except at F
B. Negative before B, 0 at B, positive between B and G, 0 at G, negative between G and E, 0 at E, then very positive at F
C. Positive before B, 0 at B, negative between B and G, 0 at G, positive between G and E, 0 at E, then very negative at F
D. Positive before B, 0 at B, negative between B and E, 0 at E, then very negative at F

C. Positive before B, 0 at B, negative between B and G, 0 at G, positive between G and E, 0 at E, then very negative at F

f′ is positive before B, crosses 0 at B, is negative between B and G, crosses 0 at G, is positive between G and E, crosses 0 at E, then is very negative at F.

Use the signs from part (a).

2. The Derivative from Tables and Formulas

3 lecture · 5 textbook · 1 past exam questions

Lecture Question · Ex 4
Table 2.6 gives values of c(t), the concentration (mg/cc) of a drug in the bloodstream at time t (min). Construct a table of estimated values for c′(t), the rate of change of c(t) with respect to t.
t (min)00.10.20.30.40.5
c(t) (mg/cc)0.840.890.940.981.001.00
t (min)0.60.70.80.91.0
c(t) (mg/cc)0.970.900.790.630.41
a. Using the average rate of change to the right (Δt = 0.1), estimate c′(0), c′(0.1), c′(0.2).
A. 0.5, 0.4, 0.2
B. 0.5, 0.5, 0.4
C. 0.89, 0.94, 0.98
D. 0.05, 0.05, 0.04

B. 0.5, 0.5, 0.4

c′(0) ≈ (0.89 − 0.84)/0.1 = 0.5; c′(0.1) ≈ (0.94 − 0.89)/0.1 = 0.5; c′(0.2) ≈ (0.98 − 0.94)/0.1 = 0.4.

Divide the change by 0.1.

b. Using the same method, estimate c′(0.6) and c′(0.9).
A. −0.07 and −0.22
B. 0.7 and 2.2
C. −0.7 and −2.2
D. −0.3 and −1.6

C. −0.7 and −2.2

c′(0.6) ≈ (0.90 − 0.97)/0.1 = −0.7; c′(0.9) ≈ (0.41 − 0.63)/0.1 = −2.2.

Divide the change by 0.1.

c. What does the table of c′ tell you about the concentration?
A. c′ < 0 for t = 0 to 0.3 (c decreasing), c′(0.4) ≈ 0; c′ > 0 for t = 0.5 to 0.9 (c increasing)
B. c′ > 0 for every t, so c is always increasing
C. c′ > 0 for t = 0 to 0.7 (c increasing); c′ < 0 after t = 0.7
D. c′ > 0 for t = 0 to 0.3 (c increasing), c′(0.4) ≈ 0; c′ < 0 for t = 0.5 to 0.9 (c decreasing)

D. c′ > 0 for t = 0 to 0.3 (c increasing), c′(0.4) ≈ 0; c′ < 0 for t = 0.5 to 0.9 (c decreasing)

c′: 0.5, 0.5, 0.4, 0.2, 0.0, −0.3, −0.7, −1.1, −1.6, −2.2. The derivative has small positive values up until t = 0.3, about 0 at t = 0.4, then it gets more and more negative: c is increasing from t = 0 to 0.4 and decreasing from t = 0.5 to 0.9.

Look at the signs of c′.

d. Improve the estimate of c′(0.2) by averaging the slopes to the left and right.
A. ≈ 0.9
B. ≈ 0.45
C. ≈ 0.4
D. ≈ 0.5

B. ≈ 0.45

c′(0.2) ≈ ½((0.94 − 0.89)/0.1 + (0.98 − 0.94)/0.1) = (0.5 + 0.4)/2 = 0.45.

Average the left and right slopes.

Lecture Question · Ex 5
Guess a formula for the derivative of f(x) = x².
f′(x) = ?
A. 2x
B. x²
C. 2
D. x

A. 2x

Using difference quotients: f′(1) ≈ ((1.001)² − 1²)/0.001 = 2; f′(2) ≈ ((2.001)² − 2²)/0.001 = 4; f′(3) ≈ ((3.001)² − 3²)/0.001 = 6. f′(1) = 2, f′(2) = 4, f′(3) = 6 suggest that f′(x) = 2x.

Estimate f′(1), f′(2), f′(3) and look for a pattern.

Lecture Question · Ex 6
Let R(x) = 100(1.1)ˣ. Using slopes to the left and right of 0, estimate R′(0).
R′(0) ≈ ?
A. ≈ 110
B. ≈ 0.0953
C. ≈ 9.53
D. ≈ 10

C. ≈ 9.53

Left (−0.001 ≤ x ≤ 0): (100(1.1)⁰ − 100(1.1)^−0.001)/0.001 ≈ 9.53. Right (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.001): (100(1.1)^0.001 − 100(1.1)⁰)/0.001 ≈ 9.53. Average of the two slopes: R′(0) ≈ 9.53.

Use tiny intervals on both sides of 0.

Textbook Question · Problem 8

x012345678

A. 5, 3, −9

Using the average rate of change to the right (Δx = 1): f′(0) ≈ (13 − 18)/1 = −5; f′(1) ≈ (10 − 13)/1 = −3. At x = 8 there is no value to the right, so we use the interval to the left: f′(8) ≈ (30 − 21)/1 = 9.

Right interval, except at the last point.

b. Where is the rate of change of f(x) positive? Where is it negative?
A. Negative for 0 ≤ x < 3 and positive for x > 3 (f′(3) ≈ 0)
B. Negative for 0 ≤ x < 5 and positive for x > 5
C. Positive for every x
D. Positive for 0 ≤ x < 3 and negative for x > 3 (f′(3) ≈ 0)

A. Negative for 0 ≤ x < 3 and positive for x > 3 (f′(3) ≈ 0)

f′: −5, −3, −1, 0, 2, 4, 6, 9, 9. The rate of change is negative for 0 ≤ x < 3 and positive for x > 3 (f′(3) ≈ 0).

Look at the signs of f′.

c. Where does the rate of change of f(x) seem to be greatest?

B. At x = 0 (f′ ≈ −5)
C. Near x = 5 (f′ ≈ 4)

D. At the right end, near x = 7 to 8 (f′ ≈ 9)

The rate of change seems to be greatest at the right end, near x = 7 to 8 (f′ ≈ 9).

Largest f′ value.

Textbook Question · Problem 9
Find approximate values for f′(x) at each of the x-values given in the following table.
x05101520
f(x)10070554640
f′(0), f′(5), f′(10), f′(15), f′(20) ≈ ?
A. −30, −15, −9, −6, −6

C. −6, −3, −1.8, −1.2, 0
D. −6, −3, −1.8, −1.2, −1.2
